title: Looking for Life on Other Worlds
summary: How scientists search for life beyond Earth by following water to Mars, to icy moons like Europa, and to planets around other stars, and why tough life on Earth gives them hope.
poll: Scientists will find life on another world in my lifetime.

versions.title: Is Life Out There?
versions.text:
Look up at the sky at night. Is there life out there? No one knows yet.

To find life, we look for water. All life we know needs it. Plants need it. You need it, too.

Mars is a red planet. Long ago, it had lakes. It had rivers, too. Now it is dry and cold. Did life live there? A rover went to find out. It is a robot car. It rolls on Mars. It picks up bits of rock. Some rocks may hold signs of life. It would be tiny life from long ago.

Jupiter is a big planet. It has a moon called Europa. The moon is cold. It has a thick shell of ice. Under the ice is a big sea! Could small things live in it? A ship from Earth is on its way to look.

There are more planets far, far off. They go round other stars. We know of lots of them! A big telescope in space looks at them. It checks the air on them. Some gas could be a sign of life.

On Earth, small things live in hot springs. They live in deep, dark seas. Life is tough. So we keep on looking.

On a clear night, you can see thousands of stars. Is anything alive out there? So far, no one has found life beyond Earth. But scientists are busy looking.

To search for life, scientists first look for water. Every living thing on Earth needs water. Tiny germs need it. Tall palm trees need it, too.

It drives over the ground. It drills into rocks and saves small bits. These rocks may hold signs of tiny life from long ago.

Jupiter is the biggest planet. One of its moons is called Europa. It has a thick shell of ice. Under the ice is a huge ocean of salt water! Could tiny living things swim in it? A spaceship from Earth is on its way to study it.

There are also planets far away. They go around other stars. Scientists have found more than five thousand of them! A giant telescope in space studies some of them. It checks the gases around each planet. Some gases could be a sign of life.

On Earth, tiny living things live in boiling hot springs and deep, dark seas. Life can be very tough. That is one reason scientists keep looking.

versions.title: Looking for Life in Space
versions.text:
On a clear night far from city lights, you can see thousands of stars. People have long wondered if anything lives out there. So far, no one has found life beyond Earth. But scientists are searching harder than ever.

To search for life, scientists first look for liquid water. Every living thing on Earth needs water, from tiny germs to tall date palms. Places with water are the best places to start.

Mars, the red planet, is our neighbor. Billions of years ago, it had rivers and lakes. Today it is dry, dusty, and freezing cold. Did life ever exist there? To find out, scientists sent a rover named Perseverance. A rover is a robot car that drives across the ground. It drills into rocks and stores small samples. These rocks may hold signs of tiny life from long ago.

Jupiter is the largest planet in our solar system. One of its moons, Europa, is covered with a thick shell of ice. Below the ice lies a huge ocean of salty water! Could tiny creatures live in it? A spaceship from Earth is traveling there now to study this moon.

There are also planets far away. They go around other stars. Scientists have discovered more than five thousand of them! A powerful telescope in space studies some of these planets. It checks the gases around them. Certain gases could be a sign of life.

On Earth, tiny living things survive in boiling hot springs and deep, dark seas. If life is that tough here, it might survive somewhere else, too.

versions.title: Looking for Life on Other Worlds
versions.text:
For thousands of years, people have looked at the night sky and wondered if we are alone. Today, scientists are using robots, spacecraft, and giant telescopes to search for an answer. So far, they have not found life anywhere except Earth. But they have found some exciting places to look.

The first clue scientists look for is liquid water. Every living thing on Earth needs it, from tiny microbes to camels. Microbes are living things so small that you need a microscope to see them. If life exists on other worlds, scientists think it will most likely be microbes.

Mars is a good place to start. Billions of years ago, it had rivers and lakes. Today it is a cold, dry desert. In 2021, a rover called Perseverance landed in a crater that once held a lake. It drills into rocks and seals small samples in tubes. Scientists are searching these rocks for evidence, or proof, that microbes once lived there.

Some moons may have water, too. Jupiter's moon Europa has a huge salty ocean hidden under its icy shell. A spacecraft called Europa Clipper launched in 2024 to study it. Saturn's moon Enceladus shoots jets of water into space from cracks in its ice.

Scientists have also found more than five thousand planets circling other stars. A few are in the habitable zone. That is the area around a star where it is not too hot or too cold for liquid water. The James Webb Space Telescope can study the atmosphere, or layer of gases, around some of these planets.

On Earth, microbes live in boiling springs and on the dark sea floor. This tells scientists that life can be tough, and it keeps them searching.

versions.title: The Search for Life Beyond Earth
versions.text:
For thousands of years, people have gazed at the night sky and wondered whether humanity is alone in the universe. Today, that question belongs to a science called astrobiology, the study of whether life exists beyond Earth and how it might begin. Using robots, spacecraft, and enormous telescopes, astrobiologists have not yet found life anywhere except our own planet, but they have identified several promising places to investigate.

The first clue researchers look for is liquid water, because every living thing on Earth depends on it, from microscopic microbes to camels. If life exists elsewhere, scientists suspect it will most likely be microbial rather than large and complex. Their confidence comes partly from extremophiles, organisms on Earth that thrive in extreme conditions such as boiling hot springs, acidic lakes, and the dark ocean floor.

Mars is a logical place to begin. Billions of years ago, it had flowing rivers and lakes, although today it is a freezing, dry desert. In 2021, the Perseverance rover landed in a crater that once contained a lake, and it has been drilling into rocks and sealing samples in tubes. Scientists are examining these rocks for biosignatures, which are chemical or physical traces that living things leave behind.

Several moons may also contain water. Jupiter's moon Europa appears to have a subsurface ocean, meaning an enormous body of salty water hidden beneath its icy shell. A spacecraft called Europa Clipper launched in 2024 to investigate it. Saturn's moon Enceladus sprays jets of water into space through fractures in its frozen surface.

Astronomers have also confirmed more than five thousand exoplanets, which are planets that orbit stars other than our Sun. A few of them travel within the habitable zone, the region around a star where temperatures allow liquid water. The James Webb Space Telescope can analyze the atmosphere surrounding some of these worlds, searching for combinations of gases that living things might produce.

Other scientists take a different approach. They use radio telescopes to listen for signals that an intelligent civilization might send. Although they have scanned many stars for decades, they have never received a message that could not be explained by natural causes or human technology.

Because life on Earth has proven so resilient, many scientists believe the search is worth continuing, even if the answer takes generations to find.

For thousands of years, people have gazed at the night sky and contemplated whether humanity is alone in the universe. Today, that ancient question belongs to a scientific discipline called astrobiology, the study of whether life exists beyond Earth and how it might originate. Using robotic explorers, spacecraft, and enormous telescopes, astrobiologists have not yet detected life anywhere except our own planet, but they have identified several promising locations to investigate.

The first clue researchers look for is liquid water, because every living thing on Earth depends on it, from microscopic microbes to camels. If life exists elsewhere, scientists suspect it will most likely be microbial rather than large and complex, and their confidence derives partly from extremophiles, organisms on Earth that flourish in extraordinarily harsh environments such as boiling hot springs, acidic lakes, and the perpetually dark ocean floor.

Mars is a logical place to begin, because billions of years ago it possessed flowing rivers and lakes, although today it is a frigid, arid desert. In 2021, the Perseverance rover landed in a crater that once contained a lake, and it has been drilling into rocks and sealing samples in tubes so that scientists can examine them for biosignatures, which are chemical or physical traces that living organisms leave behind.

Several moons may also harbor water. Jupiter's moon Europa appears to have a subsurface ocean, meaning an enormous body of salty water concealed beneath its icy shell, and a spacecraft called Europa Clipper launched in 2024 to investigate it. Meanwhile, Saturn's moon Enceladus ejects jets of water into space through fractures in its frozen surface.

Astronomers have also confirmed more than five thousand exoplanets, which are planets that orbit stars other than our Sun. A few of them travel within the habitable zone, the region around a star where temperatures permit liquid water. Other researchers pursue a different strategy, employing radio telescopes to listen for signals that an intelligent civilization might transmit. questions.stem: Why do extremophiles give scientists confidence?
options: They have been found living on Mars.
They show life can survive in conditions like those on other worlds.
They produce the very same gases that the Webb telescope is measuring.
They prove that every planet has life.
questions.why: Because extremophiles thrive in boiling springs, acidic lakes, and dark ocean floors, life might also survive harsh places beyond Earth.

wrong.A: They live on Earth; no life has been found on Mars.
wrong.C: The article does not link them to Webb's measurements.
wrong.D: The article makes no such claim.

questions.stem: Why does the author explain the habitable zone right after mentioning exoplanets?
options: To show why only some exoplanets are good targets in the search for life
To argue that all exoplanets are too hot
To describe how new stars are born inside huge, cold clouds of gas and dust
To explain how rovers land safely
questions.why: Only planets where liquid water is possible are strong candidates, so the definition shows why a few planets stand out.

wrong.B: Some exoplanets are in the habitable zone, so not all are too hot.
wrong.D: Rover landings are not connected to this idea.

questions.stem: What can you infer about why Perseverance landed in a crater that once contained a lake?
options: Craters are the warmest places on Mars today.
Lakes still exist inside Martian craters.
Scientists wanted the rover to collect water for future astronauts to drink.
Where water once existed, traces of past microbes are more likely.
questions.why: Water is the first clue for life, so an ancient lake bed is a likely place to find biosignatures.

wrong.A: The article calls Mars a freezing desert.
wrong.B: The article says the crater once held a lake.
wrong.C: The rover collects rock samples, not drinking water.

questions.stem: Based on the final paragraph, what can you infer about how scientists view the search?
options: They expect to find a final answer within the next few weeks.
They believe it is valuable even if it takes a very long time.
They think it should end because nothing has been found.
They believe only robots should continue the work.
questions.why: The article says the search is worth continuing even if the answer takes generations.

wrong.A: The article mentions generations, not weeks.
wrong.C: Scientists believe the search should continue.
wrong.D: Robots are not described as the only option.

HIGH.prompt: Scientists use rovers, spacecraft, and telescopes to search for life. Which approach do you think is most likely to succeed first? Support your answer with evidence from the article and explain one limitation of your choice.
checklist: I chose one approach and stated my claim clearly.
I supported my claim with specific evidence from the article.
I explained one limitation of my choice.
